summary: Defines a new network address format and rules for using some existing network address formats, so that OSI applications can work over non-OSI lower layers. It was on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: An OSI directory entry holds a network address that says where an end system is. This RFC makes that address carry everything needed to reach the system even when the network underneath is TCP/IP or X.25 rather than the OSI network service. It defines a new address layout, with the network identity in the first part and the network specific details, such as the IP address, in the second.

subtitle: A way to carry TCP/IP and X.25 addressing inside OSI network addresses.

tldr.problem: The OSI Directory identifies an end system by a Network Address, but OSI applications often run over lower layers such as TCP/IP or X.25, and there is no directory service that says which address to use or how to reach it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new Network Address format whose Initial Domain Part names the address family and the network, and whose Domain Specific Part carries a prefix and the network specific information, including the IP address, port and transport set for TCP/IP and the DTE number for X.25.
tldr.outcome: Everything the network needs below the transport layer can then be read out of the address itself, so an OSI application can run over a non-OSI network without a transport bridge or a directory service that resolves addresses.

today:
RFC 1277 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the Standards Track document for this encoding.

The memo records that it was originally published as UCL Research Note RN/89/13 and as a project THORN internal document, that the proposal has been implemented and the viability of the solution demonstrated, and that the assigned values are now in widespread use. Appendix A delegates the Internet space, prefix 03, to IANA.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The OSI Directory specifies an encoding of Presentation Address that uses OSI Network Addresses as defined in the OSI Network Layer standards. The directory, and any OSI application using it, must be able to use these Network Addresses to identify end systems. OSI applications are often run over lower layers other than the OSI Network Service, and it is neither reasonable nor desirable for groups wishing to investigate and use OSI applications together with the OSI Directory to depend on a global OSI Network Service. This RFC defines a new network address format, and rules for using some existing network address formats, so that the addressing information can be encoded inside the Network Address itself.

Support is defined for the RFC 1006 mapping of the Connection Oriented Transport Service onto TCP/IP, and for COTS mapped onto X.25(1980). Where an OSI application is run over CLNS on the Internet, the NSAP Guidelines of RFC 1237 should be followed instead. The document says it must be read in the context of ISO 8348 Addendum 2, and that it is not meaningful on its own.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory entry in the OSI world holds a network address, and that address is what the network uses to reach the system. This RFC asks that the address carry all the information the network needs, so that an OSI program can work over an ordinary TCP/IP or X.25 network.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
When the OSI Directory is used, the OSI location of an end system is determined by a Network Address taken from a Presentation Address and looked up in the directory. OSI applications are currently operated over several kinds of lower layer: an international X.25 network that routes on the basis of X.121 addresses, mostly X.25(80) but with some X.25(84) that carries Network Addresses as user data; large private X.25 networks without DNICs; isolated networks running the Connection Oriented Network Service; isolated networks running the Connectionless Network Service; the CLNP pilot taking place in the NSFNet and NORDUNet communities; isolated TCP/IP LANs using RFC 1006; and the DARPA/NSF Internet.

In general these systems have to be interconnected by the use of transport bridging or application relaying. Transport bridging causes a number of problems that are better avoided, and only some applications can support relaying, which is not always satisfactory.

The intended OSI solution is a single global network service, with globally allocated Network Addresses that imply nothing about routing or location. An End System is attached to one or more subnetworks at Subnetwork Points of Attachment, and Intermediate Systems join subnetworks in the same way. Routing is achieved by repeated binding of a Network Address to an SNPA, first at the Originating End System and then at each Intermediate System, using network level routing mechanisms. That only works in a pure OSI environment with a single ubiquitous network service, so it does not solve the problem this document addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: OSI applications run over many different networks, and joining those networks together normally needs a bridge at the transport layer or a relay at the application layer, both of which cause trouble. The address itself is the only thing an application has to work with, so the fix has to be in the address.

sections.title: The General Approach
sections.content:
Connecting to a remote Application Entity broadly works in four steps. The Application Entity is looked up in the OSI Directory to obtain a Presentation Address. Each Network Address in that Presentation Address is extracted, and it is determined whether it can be used and how. An order of preference is determined for those Network Addresses. One or more of them is then tried.

This document is concerned with the second step, and will probably have implications for the third. There is currently no directory service to provide step 2, so this interim approach has to be algorithmic. All the addressing information the network requires must be extracted from the Network Address.

Two kinds of Network Address are discussed: the use of X.121 form Network Addresses, and a special encoding of Telex form Network Addresses. An Application Entity should strictly have only one Presentation Address, but in practice it may have several, and the network addresses of each Presentation Address should be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: Reaching a remote system normally means looking it up in the directory, then working out which of the addresses in the entry can actually be used and in what order to try them. There is no service that does the second part for you, so the rules have to be written into the address format itself.

sections.title: The New Network Address Format
sections.content:
The scope of the new format is any TCP/IP network supporting COTS using RFC 1006, and any mapping of COTS onto X.25, usually X.25(80), where X.25 is not used to provide CONS, so that only the DTE and not a Network address is carried. The exceptions are the cases handled by the X.121 AFI in Section 3. The intention is to use the X.121 AFI wherever possible, and the formats defined in this section are for the remaining cases.

Six requirements govern the new format. The information for the layers below Transport must be obtainable from the Network Address, because the Network Address is the information available. The Network Addresses must be globally unique, since they can be looked up by anyone with access to the Directory. The address should be allocated so that confusion with a real network address, one that defines an NSAP using CONS or CLNS rather than X.25(80) or RFC 1006, is unlikely. The address must be interpretable on the basis of well known information, or of information obtainable from the OSI Directory, and this document only uses well known information. The identity of the network must be deducible from the Network Address. And all network specific addressing information, including the SNPA, must be deducible from the Network Address.

The IDP is used with the Telex AFI, chosen because it gives the largest DSP and because it is less likely than other forms to be used for real network addresses. The Local, X.121, DCC and ICD AFIs might have been chosen, but are not used: Local would not give globally unique values, and the others may be confused with other uses of OSI network addresses. The IDI should be assigned in a manner appropriate to the use of the encoding, and for a private network within an organisation the telex number of that organisation would be a good choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The new address has two halves. The first half says what kind of address this is and who issued it. The second half says which network it belongs to and how to reach the system on that network. Six rules make sure the address can always be read without asking anyone.

sections.title: The Domain Specific Part Encoding
sections.content:
The network address is used so that a subnetwork is identified by the IDP and a small part of the DSP, and the remainder of the DSP encodes network specific information. The top level format is independent of the means used to provide COTS, and two formats for the remainder of the DSP are then defined for particular ways of providing it.

A decimal abstract encoding is defined for the DSP. The ECMA 117 format might have been used, but it is not suitable. A binary encoding, with the DSP structured in ASN.1, would have been a very attractive approach, but there is insufficient space in the Network Address for that to be feasible. The structure that is defined has a two digit prefix and a network specific part of up to 27 digits. The two digit prefix allows multiple uses of the same DSP without consuming all of it, and allows the DSP to be used with different encodings. The network specific allocation should be less than 20 digits if the structure is to be used with any IDI format, and this is increased to 27 for the Telex format.

The IDP together with the two digit prefix identify a subnetwork in which the value of the remainder of the DSP, the Network Specific Part, is to be interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: The second half of the address starts with two digits that name the network, and the digits after it hold whatever that network needs. The whole thing is written in decimal, because there is not enough room in an address to hold it in binary form.

sections.title: X.25(80) Network Specific Format
sections.content:
The IDP and prefix identify an X.25(80) subnetwork. There is a need to represent a DTE Number, and optionally an X.25 Protocol ID or CUDF, which many implementations require because of the shortage of X.121 address space, in the DSP. This is structured in one of two possible ways: either a DTE number alone, or a type field, a length in octets for the PID or CUDF, the PID or CUDF itself, and the DTE number.

The Type field has the values 0 for DTE only, 1 for DTE plus PID, 2 for DTE plus CUDF, and 3 to 9 reserved. The PID or CUDF takes as many digits as three times the length in octets, each octet being encoded as three decimal digits that represent its decimal value. The DTE is terminated by the end of the Network Address.

The document works through an example: the JANET DTE 000005111600 with the ASCII CUDF "12". In the concrete binary form, which the document calls the syntax most likely to be used in practice, octets are written in hexadecimal, and the two CUDF octets 049 and 050 map to six digits.
sections.plainLanguage: On an X.25 network the address has to carry the number of the data terminal, and often also a protocol identifier or a user data field. The address starts with a one digit type that says which of those it holds, and the rest of the digits are the terminal number.

sections.title: TCP/IP (RFC 1006) Network Specific Format
sections.content:
The IDP and the two digit prefix identify a TCP/IP network where RFC 1006 is applied. An IP Address has to be used, because there are insufficient bits to fit in a domain. The structure has three fields: an IP address, an optional port number, and a transport set that indicates what kind of IP-based transport protocol is used.

The port number can be up to 65535 and needs 5 digits; it is optional and is defaulted as defined in RFC 1006. The transport set is a decimal number from 0 to 65535, which is really a 16-bit flag word, where 1 is TCP and 2 is UDP, with further values of this code assigned by IANA. If the transport set is not there, or no bits are set, it means the default, which is TCP. It is encoded in 5 digits.

The example in the document is the IP Address 10.0.0.6 with port 9 over UDP, written with the Telex IDI 007 28722, the prefix 03, the address as 010 000 000 006, the port as 00009 and the transport set as 00002.
sections.plainLanguage: On a TCP/IP network the address holds three things in order: the IP address, the port number, and a number that says whether the traffic uses TCP or UDP. The port and the transport number may be left out, in which case the defaults apply.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says plainly that security considerations are not discussed in it. It does set out related requirements in Section 4.1: the Network Addresses must be globally unique, because they can be looked up by anyone with access to the OSI Directory, and the address should be allocated so that confusion with a real network address, one that defines an NSAP using CONS or CLNS, is unlikely.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo has no security section, because it is about how addresses are laid out rather than about protecting them. What it does say is that anyone with access to the directory can read the address, and that the numbers chosen should not be mistaken for addresses belonging to a real OSI network.
